title: "Truth alone prevails" — satyam eva jayate (3.1)
hook: three words from the Mundaka sit beneath India's national emblem, and the verse they come from keeps going
tomorrow: not by eye, not by speech

segments.voice: Yesterday: the two birds on one tree, suparna, and your line, the one who watches. Did you look up, once, at the bird on the same branch? Day four hundred eighteen.

If you've ever held Indian money, you've held this lesson. Look at the national emblem: the lions, back to back, taken from a pillar of the emperor Ashoka. Underneath them, in Devanagari script, three words. Satyameva jayate. Truth alone prevails. They're on Indian money, on government seals and documents. And they come from the Mundaka Upanishad, from the chapter we're reading right now. And the full verse says a good deal more than the emblem has room for.
screen: `THE LIONS OF ASHOKA'S PILLAR.` → `SATYAMEVA JAYATE.` → `FROM THE MUNDAKA UPANISHAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the first line of the verse: satyam eva jayate, nanritam. Truth alone wins, not untruth. Satya, truth, comes from sat, what is, what's real. So truth here is more than accurate words. It's being in line with what actually is. Eva means only, alone. And nanritam, not anritam: anrita is the crooked, the false, the opposite of rita, the right order of things. So: what is real wins. What's crooked doesn't. Then the verse keeps going, and this is the part the coins leave off. By truth the road is laid out, the path of the gods, on which the sages travel, their desires fulfilled, to the place where truth's highest treasure is. So truth isn't only the winner of an argument. It's a road. You walk on it, and it takes you somewhere. That fits the neighboring verses. Just before this, the Mundaka says the self is reached by truth, by austerity, by right knowledge, by the steady life of a student. Truthfulness isn't a rule stuck on the outside of spiritual life. It's the pavement. The words became the motto beneath the national emblem when India became a republic, in 1950. It's a hopeful choice for a country's seal. It doesn't claim that truth wins quickly, or every day, or in every courtroom. The Upanishad's claim is longer and quieter. Over the whole road, what is real holds, and what's crooked doesn't.
screen: `TRUTH ALONE WINS, NOT UNTRUTH.` · `SATYA: WHAT IS REAL.` · `BY TRUTH THE ROAD IS LAID.` · `A REPUBLIC'S MOTTO, 1950.` · then, large: `SATYAMEVA JAYATE.`

segments.voice: Two minutes on the road of truth. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then bring to mind one small place in your life where something is a little crooked: a fib you told to keep the peace, a thing you said you'd do and didn't, a story you tell yourself that isn't quite so. No shame. Just look at it plainly. Then picture what it would be like to set that one stone straight. Rest in that picture. The bell holds the time.
Satya, truth, what is real. Satyam eva jayate, from Mundaka 3.1: truth alone wins, not untruth, and by truth the road of the gods is laid.
Your line: the motto on the coins. Today, the next time you handle money, let it remind you of three words, and straighten one small crooked thing. Day four hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: Satyameva jayate is printed beneath India's national emblem on currency and official documents, and Hindu teachers and families quote it as a reminder that truthfulness is part of dharma.

original.note: Sanskrit satyam eva jayate: truth alone wins. Mundaka 3.1.6; India's national motto.

trapdoor: what you thought: it's a slogan, like 'honesty is the best policy'.
what it means: what is real wins, not the crooked; and truth is a road that leads to its own highest treasure.
what a scholar hears: satyena panthā vitato devayānaḥ (3.1.6): the devayana, the path of the gods, which tradition links with the northern path the Prashna described.

sources.ref: Mundaka Upanishad 3.1.5 (the self reached by truth, discipline, right knowledge)
State Emblem of India, adopted 26 January 1950

notes: Verse numbering: satyam eva jayate is 3.1.6 in most editions. Confirm.

Emblem facts: adopted 26 January 1950, motto in Devanagari beneath the Lion Capital of Ashoka at Sarnath. Confirm, and confirm the motto appears on Indian coins as well as banknotes (the carry, fixed by the index, says 'coins'; some coin series show the emblem without the motto).
Malaviya popularizing the phrase is commonly stated (e.g. at the 1918 Congress session); hedged as 'many people credit'. Confirm or cut.
Etymology: satya from sat; anrta as the negation of rta. Standard; confirm.
Some manuscripts/readings give jayati for jayate; not raised in the script.

Editor review 2026-10-01: cut 'millions carry them' and 'far fewer know' (unsourced counts) from the hook and the 'most people' teaser; cut the Malaviya attribution (unverified); 3.1.5 list corrected to truth, austerity (tapas), right knowledge and brahmacharya (was 'discipline ... a disciplined life'); devayana-northern path link now hedged as tradition.
